argument: Stoicism grew out of cynicism but insisted that ethics could not stand alone -- it needed a physics and a logic to justify it, since living virtuously in agreement with nature requires first knowing what nature actually is. Zeno of Citium, shaped by a shipwreck and his cynic training under Crates, built a materialist, pantheistic system in which God, nature, and the universe are identical, animated by an active divine reason (logos) that governs passive matter and produces fate. Humans participate in that reason, and the whole point of logic and physics is to let people reason well enough to live in harmony with this providential, deterministic universe.
keyIdeas: The stoics pictured logic, physics, and ethics as an egg's shell, yolk, and white: distinct but interdependent, so ethics can't be properly understood without the physics and logic that ground it.

Stoicism evolved directly out of cynicism (Zeno studied under the cynic Crates), keeping the cynic emphasis on virtue and living according to nature but adding the physics and metaphysics cynicism lacked.

The stoic universe is pantheistic: God is not a being outside the universe but the material universe itself, divided into passive nature (raw matter) and active nature (the divine logos/reason that shapes it).

Because reason has had infinite tries at creating and destroying the universe in an eternal cycle and always does it the one perfect way, everything that happens is fated, and accepting that fate rationally is the path to tranquility.

Zeno's hand-gesture demonstration (open palm, closing fingers, closed fist, fist gripped by the other hand) visualized perception, assent, comprehension, and knowledge as increasing degrees of epistemic certainty.
